data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism constructs a false dichotomy between 'getting closer to the truth' and 'eliminating more errors,' treating them as distinct outcomes. But within the Popperian framework the target is critiquing, verisimilitude is literally defined as increasing truth content while decreasing falsity content — so 'eliminating more errors' IS the operationalization of 'getting closer to truth.' By asserting 'we can never say we are getting closer to the truth, only that we have eliminated more errors,' the target severs two concepts that are definitionally identical in the framework under discussion. This makes the central claim — that accepting the wager 'costs science its claim to progressive convergence toward truth' — internally incoherent: the very process the target concedes survives (error elimination) is the mechanism of convergence. The target even acknowledges this tension in countercondition 1, where it admits that if verisimilitude can be rigorously defined, 'the cost of losing convergence is paid back' — but verisimilitude IS the formalization of the error-elimination process the target already grants as surviving. The argument thus relies on treating a single concept as two, inflating the 'cost' of the wager into a loss of convergence that was never actually lost.
